questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify the opening that names a disagreement
questions.stem: In a design review the lead opens by noting that two groups disagree about load paths. Which opening best names the disagreement plainly?

options.text: The two positions in conflict are named explicitly, so reviewers can see where the real clash lies.
The opening announces the project phase so every reviewer knows the schedule before discussion starts.
options.misconception: treats a shared agenda item as a stated disagreement

options.text: The opening asserts the engineer's own preferred structure and sets the direction for the whole review.
options.misconception: assumes the speaker's own side is the only valid one

options.text: The opening asks the client to approve the current design at once, moving the meeting straight to a decision.
options.misconception: believes naming a disagreement means demanding a verdict

questions.explanation: Option A points at the two positions in conflict, which is what naming a disagreement requires. B reports timing instead, C argues a side, and D turns description into a demand.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence shows where the parties differ.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a counterargument aim at the stated claim
questions.stem: A reviewer's counterargument attacks a decision the design team never questioned. Explain what makes that reply miss its target and what a reply aimed at the stated claim would need to say.

answer.exemplar: The reply attacks a side issue that nobody in the brief defended, so it leaves the team's actual proposal untouched. A reply aimed at the stated claim would name the claim about the support spacing, cite the assumption it rests on, and explain why that assumption fails under the loads the brief describes.

questions.explanation: A counterargument must take up the words of the claim it answers, so the reply should name the claim and show why it fails, not the nearest thing that is easy to attack.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim actually says before attacking it.

questions.hint: Separate what the memo reports from what the memo chooses.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Interruption that helps and interruption that does not
questions.learningObjective: Explain when an interruption advances a discussion
questions.stem: During a fault review an engineer interrupts a colleague mid-sentence to point out that a load figure contradicts an earlier one. Explain when that interruption helps the discussion and when it does not.

answer.exemplar: The interruption helps when it names a specific contradiction that the speaker could not see, because it shortens the path to correcting the figure. It does not help when it merely cuts the speaker off, delivers the correction as a verdict, or takes over the argument before the speaker has stated the position.

questions.explanation: An interruption is helpful when it adds a point the speaker could not add and is unhelpful when it only cuts the speaker off or substitutes the interrupter's own argument for the one in progress.
questions.hint: Ask what the interruption adds, not who made it.

answer.exemplar: The comment presents a conclusion as the only remaining option while appearing to ask for confirmation, which pressures the team into accepting it. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between rebuttable and non-rebuttable claims
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a claim that can be answered with reasons and one that cannot, and give an example of each from a design brief.

answer.exemplar: A rebuttable claim is one where reasons could show it false, such as stating that a 300 mm beam will carry the specified load over that span. A non-rebuttable claim is one the brief treats as settled or as given, such as the maximum permitted storey height set by the approval, where the reply asks what the rule allows rather than disputing the rule.

questions.explanation: The distinction is whether reasons could change the answer. Where they could, the claim is rebuttable and disputing it is reasonable; where they could not, the reply should work inside the constraint.
questions.hint: Ask whether a good reason could change the answer.

answer.exemplar: A purely factual disagreement is settled by measurement or reference, because both parties accept the same test for the answer. questions.hint: Find the sentence in the brief that the reply must answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Disagreements about facts and about values
questions.learningObjective: Separate factual from value disagreements
questions.stem: Which engineering exchange is a disagreement about values rather than about facts?

options.text: The section depth in the calculation is 450 mm, while the brief's table shows 400 mm.
options.misconception: mistakes a record discrepancy for a conflict of values

options.text: The specified concrete fails the cover requirement in the exposure class stated in the brief.
options.misconception: calls a compliance finding a matter of personal preference

options.text: The wind pressure differs between two assessments of the same site and height.
options.misconception: treats conflicting estimates as a disagreement of preference

options.text: The team prefers a deep open-plan lobby, while the client wants a cellular reception area.

questions.explanation: D sets out two different preferences for the same space, with nothing measurable in dispute. A and C are disputes about records and figures, and B is a compliance finding.
questions.hint: Ask which pair of statements shares no measurable gap.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain how tone can close a discussion
questions.stem: Explain how the tone of a reply can close a discussion even when the reply contains no argument at all.

answer.exemplar: A reply can close a discussion through dismissiveness, sarcasm, impatience, or the announcement that the speaker has stopped listening, because these signal to everyone present that contributing is pointless or unwelcome. The claims may all be reasonable, but the manner withdraws the invitation to continue, so the disagreement ends without being resolved.

questions.explanation: Tone signals whether contributing is welcome, so it controls how a discussion continues whatever the words say. Dismissiveness, sarcasm and a refusal to listen end an argument without answering it.
questions.hint: Ask what the manner tells the other people present.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a disagreement is actually named

stimulus.body: Item 4: The drainage team and the landscaping team both accept the levels as surveyed. Item 5: The landscaping team says the pool coping must sit flush with the terrace, and the drainage team says the terrace cannot take the overflow route without a 30 mm step. Item 6: It was noted that items 1 to 3 were closed.

questions.stem: Which item contains a named disagreement?

options.text: Item 5, because it sets out two requirements that cannot both be met at the same location.
Item 6, because it records that several items were closed during the meeting.
options.misconception: mistakes a record of closure for a statement of conflict

options.text: Item 4, because it mentions two teams agreeing on the same surveyed levels.
options.misconception: treats agreement as the disagreement to be named

options.text: No item names one, because the minutes record positions rather than conflicts.
options.misconception: assumes a conflict must be flagged in the wording

questions.explanation: Item 5 pairs two requirements that cannot both hold at one spot, which names the conflict. B and C misread the record, and D assumes conflicts must be labelled as such.
questions.hint: Look for two requirements that clash at one place.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Select the reply that attacks the stated claim
questions.stem: Which reply to the brief's claim about lift capacity attacks that claim itself rather than an adjacent topic?

options.text: The lift lobby needs more area, and the brief does not give it enough, which is the real problem.
options.misconception: raises a space issue as though it answered the claim

options.text: The brief assumes 40 percent of occupants arrive in one ten-minute peak, which cannot be true.
The lift supplier should confirm the figures before the brief is circulated any further.
options.misconception: proposes a source of checks instead of testing the claim

options.text: Most buildings of this size manage the same population with the same number of lifts.
options.misconception: appeals to common experience instead of the brief's figure

questions.explanation: B attacks the peak assumption the brief itself uses, so the reply would fail if the assumption held. A and D bring in other subjects, and C defers rather than argues.
questions.hint: Check which sentence of the brief the reply contradicts.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Interruption that helps and interruption that does not
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether an interruption advances the exchange
questions.stem: First judge whether the interruption in the meeting advanced the case, then choose the reply.

options.text: It advanced the case, so the speaker should thank the interrupter and end the point there.
options.misconception: ends the point when the interruption only supplied one fact

options.text: It damaged the case, so the meeting should formally record the interruption in the minutes.
options.misconception: punishes the speaker by logging a moment of confusion

options.text: It advanced the case, so the team should follow the point and rejoin the original argument.
It damaged the case, so the next speaker should restate the whole original point from the start.
options.misconception: repeats the whole argument instead of resuming it

questions.explanation: An interruption that supplies a missing point should be followed and the original argument resumed. A closes the point early, B records a non-event, and D restarts instead of continuing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the original argument can be resumed.
